title: A Proven Way To Improve Your Students’ Mental Health During Covid ntal-health-during-covid/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Amid rising pandemic-era mental health concerns, Linsin recommends a simple, research-backed intervention: getting students outside into natural sunlight, which he notes is linked to higher serotonin and lower cortisol levels. He acknowledges not every student has access to expansive nature but insists sunlight and small strips of outdoor space are available almost everywhere, and offers practical classroom applications like filming weather reports outdoors, categorizing clouds, or using the environment as a writing prompt. He frames this as one of several strategies alongside choice and kindness already covered elsewhere, but singles out sunlight for being especially easy and proven, closing with an image of running outside to reconnect students with themselves, each other, and the world.
points: Sunlight exposure is cited as scientifically linked to boosting serotonin and lowering cortisol, directly improving mood.
Even students without access to a park or yard are said to have access to some form of nature — sky, grass, a nearby creek.
Practical outdoor activities suggested include filming weather reports, categorizing clouds, identifying birds, and nature-based writing prompts.
In-person or hybrid students, while doing better than fully remote ones, are still said to benefit meaningfully from outdoor time.
The intervention is framed as one of the simplest available tools for addressing pandemic-driven student mental health issues.
quotes: Mounting research indicates a sharp increase in mental health issues among students since the pandemic began. This includes soaring rates of anxiety, depression, and suicide.
It’s easy, scientifically proven, and shown to boost serotonin (the feel-good hormone) and lower cortisol (the stress hormone).
It’s sunlight. It’s getting students outside and walking, or even sitting, in nature.

But the lift it gives your students—the energy they experience from getting out and moving and thinking and feeling the rush of life on their senses—is a balm for the soul-crush of living in dark isolation.
Students desperately need to get back to connection—with themselves, with each other, and with the wild world around them.
So take your class, electronically or otherwise, and head for the door. Run out into the world with a rebellious whoop.
